doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Eddie Condon and his Greenwich Village crowd
summary: Ingham describes Eddie Condon as a catalyst whose club drew a literate crowd in 1946, against bebop and big bands.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I see you were in on a Condon memorial thing too? Eddie Condon?

Yeah. Well that was with Bobby Gordon and we just did a little, it wasn’t a tribute or anything. Eddie Condon was a kind of a catalyst for music that’s now just completely out of any of these jazz critics or these educators would not mention Eddie Condon. I mean they think he’s absolutely beneath them. It’s a guy who was a wonderful rhythm guitar player. He didn’t play any solos. What did he do? He drank himself crazy and he was just part of the times, but he was a wonderful catalyst. He brought together so many great players. I don’t know why — that kind of music was much maligned of course. Once upon a time — it was a particular kind of a New York kind of music I thought, Eddie’s music. When he was playing, he had his own club as you know, down in Greenwich Village. In 1946 he opened up I think. And it really kind of attracted a literate crowd, maybe an ivy league kind of crowd down there. They were editors, publishers, journalists, you know kind of somewhat racy and somewhat well educated, you know, © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
Harvard people and businessmen and that. But they liked it. They liked the sound. A lot of them, like John O’Hara, the novelist, and — he wrote Cannery Row.

Steinbeck, yeah, the people who went there. I mean Condon’s was a great place. Then of course at the time bebop was there, and that was the other side of the fence. These were totally extremes. And even the big bands too, were another extreme. Because the Condon guys thought that if you worked in a big band, you were somewhat selling out, you know, you were sacrificing the jazz for commercial security. But of course there was so much work there, in New York particularly, back in ‘46, I mean there were so many places going, and there were jobs. So now there’s nothing like that at all. I mean it’s absolutely all gone. Well the times have gone. But you didn’t have to feel, if you couldn’t work there you couldn’t work somewhere else, or this was the only place to be. And I wish I’d been around in those times, I’ll tell you.
